concepts.name: Brundtland Commission Definition: Precision and Implications
key_dimensions: Exact wording: 'meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs' — UPSC often tests the precise phrase
The two key concepts embedded: 'needs' (especially of the world's poor) and 'limitations' imposed by technology and social organization
Common trap: distinguishing Brundtland Commission (Our Common Future, 1987) from Stockholm (1972) and Rio (1992) declarations
The implicit prioritization of poverty eradication within the definition — intergenerational vs. intragenerational equity

concepts.name: Three Pillars of Sustainable Development: Overlap and Tensions
key_dimensions: Economic, Social, and Environmental pillars — and the 'nexus' or intersection zones (e.g., social-economic = equity; economic-environmental = viability; social-environmental = bearability)
UPSC trap: some frameworks cite 4 pillars (adding 'Institutional/Governance') — differentiating UN DESA framework from classic Brundtland three-pillar model
Tensions between pillars: when economic growth conflicts with environmental sustainability — resource curse, green paradox
The concept of 'weak' vs. 'strong' sustainability as interpretations of how pillars relate (substitutability vs. complementarity)

concepts.name: Intergenerational Equity: Principle and Legal Status
key_dimensions: Definition: obligation of current generation not to foreclose options for future generations — associated with Edith Brown Weiss
Three planetary trust obligations: conservation of options, conservation of quality, conservation of access
Judicial recognition in India: Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) and its invocation of sustainable development as customary international law
Distinction from intragenerational equity — UPSC frequently conflates or tests the boundary between the two

concepts.name: Intragenerational Equity: Poverty, Justice, and Development
key_dimensions: Focus on present-generation disparities: between North-South, urban-rural, rich-poor — often tested as the 'social pillar' operationalization
Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR) as the international legal expression of intragenerational equity
Link to SDG Goal 10 (Reduced Inequalities) and Goal 1 (No Poverty) — how intragenerational equity is operationalized in the 2030 Agenda
UPSC trap: distinguishing CBDR (intragenerational equity between nations) from precautionary principle (risk management) — both appear together in Rio Declaration

concepts.name: Precautionary Principle: Scope, Application, and Misapplication
key_dimensions: Core formulation: when an action raises threats of harm to environment or human health, precautionary measures should be taken even if cause-and-effect relationships are not fully established scientifically
Rio Declaration Principle 15 wording vs. Wingspread Statement (1998) — stronger formulation vs. weaker formulation
Indian judicial application: Vellore Citizens case elevated it to customary international law; later cases (e.g., Narmada Bachao Andolan) show retreat from strong application
UPSC trap: precautionary principle ≠ prevention principle — the former applies under scientific uncertainty, the latter when harm is known

concepts.name: Polluter Pays Principle: Definition, Exceptions, and Indian Context
key_dimensions: OECD origin (1972): polluter should bear the cost of pollution control measures — ensures internalization of negative externalities
Extended Polluter Pays Principle (EPP) in Indian courts: goes beyond cleanup costs to include restoration and compensation to victims (Vellore Citizens, Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. UoI)
UPSC trap: PPP in environmental law vs. PPP in public finance (Public-Private Partnership) — same acronym, entirely different concepts
Limitations and exceptions: state subsidies for pollution control in developing nations, difficulty in identifying polluters in cases of diffuse/non-point source pollution

concepts.name: Carrying Capacity and Ecological Limits as Sustainability Foundations
key_dimensions: Definition: maximum population/activity level an ecosystem can support without degrading its ability to provide for future needs
Planetary Boundaries framework (Rockström et al., 2009): 9 boundaries — UPSC tests which have been transgressed (climate change, biosphere integrity, biogeochemical flows, land-system change)
Distinction: carrying capacity (population ecology concept) vs. ecological footprint (consumption measurement tool) vs. biocapacity (supply-side measure)
Policy implication: carrying capacity as a ceiling for development planning — used in Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) notifications and EIA frameworks in India

concepts.name: Sustainable Development vs. Green Growth vs. Degrowth: Conceptual Boundaries
key_dimensions: Green Growth (OECD/World Bank): economic growth while minimizing environmental costs — assumes decoupling is achievable; criticized as an oxymoron by degrowth advocates
Degrowth: planned reduction of production/consumption in high-income countries — incompatible with conventional GDP-focused development
Circular Economy as a middle path: keeps resources in use longer, eliminates waste — EU's Circular Economy Action Plan vs. India's EPR frameworks
UPSC trap: 'sustainable development' is NOT synonymous with 'green growth' — the former includes social pillar explicitly; the latter is primarily economic-environmental

concepts.name: Evolution of Sustainable Development: Stockholm to Rio+20 Milestones
key_dimensions: Stockholm Conference (1972): first UN conference on environment — established UNEP; Principle 1 on human right to environment
Brundtland Report (1987): Our Common Future — coined the modern SD definition; recommended Earth Summit
Rio Earth Summit (1992): produced Agenda 21, Rio Declaration (27 principles), CBD, UNFCCC, Forest Principles — NOT legally binding except CBD and UNFCCC

Rio+20 (2012): 'The Future We Want' outcome document — launched SDGs process, endorsed Green Economy; UPSC trap: Rio+20 did NOT adopt SDGs, it initiated the intergovernmental process that led to their adoption in 2015

concepts.name: Agenda 21 and Local Agenda 21: Structure and Implementation
key_dimensions: Agenda 21: comprehensive blueprint for global action on SD adopted at Rio 1992 — 4 sections, 40 chapters covering social/economic dimensions, conservation, major groups, means of implementation
Local Agenda 21: urges local governments to develop their own SD plans through consultation with communities — bottom-up governance principle
Chapter 28 significance: explicitly calls on local authorities to consult populations and achieve consensus on 'local Agenda 21' — UPSC tests this decentralization angle
Distinction: Agenda 21 (non-binding action plan, 1992) vs. SDGs (political commitment framework, 2015) vs. CBD (legally binding treaty, 1992)

concepts.name: SDGs vs. MDGs: Architecture, Universality, and Key Differences
key_dimensions: MDGs (2000–2015): 8 goals, 21 targets — focused on developing countries, donor-recipient framing, top-down design by UN experts
SDGs (2015–2030): 17 goals, 169 targets, 231 unique indicators — universal application (all countries), bottom-up consultative design, integrate all three pillars
UPSC trap: MDG 7 (environmental sustainability) was add-on; SDGs integrate environment across ALL 17 goals — not a separate environmental goal
Financing gap and means of implementation: SDG 17 (Partnerships) as the 'meta-goal' — Addis Ababa Action Agenda (2015) as the financing framework

concepts.name: Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR): Legal Basis and Tensions
key_dimensions: Rio Declaration Principle 7 formulation: common responsibility for global environment, differentiated based on 'different contributions to global environmental degradation' and 'different capabilities'
Two components often tested separately: common responsibility (all states must act) + differentiated responsibilities (extent of obligation varies)
CBDR in UNFCCC vs. Paris Agreement: Paris Agreement's 'CBDR-RC' (respective capabilities) formulation — subtle but significant shift that weakens historical differentiation
UPSC trap: CBDR applies to global environmental problems (climate, biodiversity) but NOT to transboundary pollution disputes — different legal framework applies there

concepts.name: Natural Capital and Ecosystem Services: Valuation Frameworks
key_dimensions: Natural capital: stock of natural assets providing ecosystem services — TEEB (The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity) framework for valuation
Four categories of ecosystem services: provisioning, regulating, cultural, supporting — UPSC tests classification and examples

Weak vs. strong sustainability interpreted through natural capital lens: weak sustainability allows substitution of natural capital with human-made capital; strong sustainability holds natural capital as non-substitutable
India-specific: National Mission for Green India, Green GDP attempts — IUCN's concept of 'nature-based solutions' as operationalization of natural capital

concepts.name: Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) as SD Tool: Process and Controversies
key_dimensions: EIA under Environment Protection Act 1986 and EIA Notification 2006 — mandatory for 'Category A' and 'Category B' projects; threshold-based classification
Post-facto clearance controversy: EIA Draft 2020 proposed legitimizing post-facto environmental clearances — criticized as violating precautionary principle and sustainable development norms
Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA): applies SD principles at policy/plan level (upstream) vs. EIA (project level) — India lacks mandatory SEA framework (UPSC trap)
Public hearing requirement as social pillar operationalization: Principle 10 of Rio Declaration (public participation) — exceptions and dilutions are frequently tested

concepts.name: Sustainable Development in Indian Constitutional Framework
key_dimensions: Article 48A (DPSP): state shall endeavor to protect and improve environment and safeguard forests and wildlife — added by 42nd Amendment 1976
Article 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty): protect and improve natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers, wildlife — duty of every citizen
Supreme Court's elevation of SD to fundamental right under Article 21: Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (right to pollution-free water and air) — linking environment to life
UPSC trap: Article 48A is non-justiciable DPSP, but courts have used it alongside Article 21 to make environmental protection justiciable — the 'harmonious construction' judicial technique

concepts.name: Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in India: Institutional Framework and Progress
key_dimensions: NITI Aayog as nodal agency for SDG implementation in India — SDG India Index and Dashboard (annual) measures state/UT-level progress
Voluntary National Review (VNR): India submitted VNRs in 2017 and 2020 to UN High-Level Political Forum — content and key findings are UPSC-relevant
Mapping SDGs to existing schemes: India's approach of aligning national programs (e.g., Jal Jeevan Mission → SDG 6; PM-KUSUM → SDG 7) rather than creating new SDG-specific programs
UPSC trap: SDG India Index scores — top and bottom performing states; the distinction between 'Achiever', 'Front Runner', 'Performer', and 'Aspirant' categories

concepts.name: Sustainable Development and Trade: WTO-Environment Interface
key_dimensions: WTO Preamble explicitly references sustainable development and optimal use of world's resources — one of the few trade agreements to do so

Article XX GATT exceptions: measures 'necessary to protect human, animal or plant life or health' (XX-b) and relating to 'conservation of exhaustible natural resources' (XX-g) — conditional exceptions
Shrimp-Turtle case (1998): WTO Appellate Body interpreted 'exhaustible natural resources' to include living species — evolutionary interpretation supporting SD

UPSC trap: WTO does NOT prohibit environmental regulations per se — it prohibits disguised trade restrictions; the 'necessity test' and 'least trade restrictive alternative' are key compliance standards

concepts.name: The Precautionary Principle vs. Science-Based Decision Making: Regulatory Tensions
key_dimensions: Core tension: precautionary principle allows action under uncertainty; science-based approaches (WTO SPS Agreement) require risk assessment before restriction — the GMO and nuclear energy debates exemplify this
Moratorium use in India: Supreme Court's de facto moratorium on Bt Brinjal (2010 onwards) as application of precautionary principle despite GEAC approval
Reverse onus principle: who bears burden of proof — traditional approach (harm must be proven) vs. precautionary approach (safety must be proven by proponent)

UPSC trap: Rio Declaration Principle 15 says precautionary approach shall be 'widely applied' by states — it does NOT make it a binding rule of customary international law in all contexts; Vellore Citizens judgment's claim remains contested internationally

concepts.name: Green Economy, Circular Economy, and Blue Economy: Definitional Distinctions
key_dimensions: Green Economy (UNEP): results in improved human well-being and social equity while significantly reducing environmental risks — low carbon, resource efficient, socially inclusive
Circular Economy: restorative and regenerative by design — eliminates waste through 'reduce, reuse, recycle' plus 'recover and redesign'; Ellen MacArthur Foundation framework
Blue Economy: sustainable use of ocean resources for economic growth — India's Blue Economy Policy 2021; distinct from 'ocean economy' which doesn't require sustainability qualifier
UPSC trap: these are NOT synonymous with sustainable development — they are specific models or pathways toward it; Green Economy ≠ Green GDP ≠ Green Growth

concepts.name: Limits to Growth Debate and Planetary Boundaries: Historical-Scientific Context
key_dimensions: Limits to Growth (Club of Rome, 1972): computer modeling showed exponential growth on finite planet leads to collapse — contested but influential; relevance to carrying capacity concept

Planetary Boundaries (Stockholm Resilience Centre, 2009, updated 2015, 2023): 9 boundaries — as of 2023, 6 of 9 have been transgressed (climate change, biosphere integrity, land-system change, freshwater change, novel entities, biogeochemical flows)
Safe Operating Space concept: the zone within all planetary boundaries where humanity can thrive — underpins the 'environmental ceiling' in Kate Raworth's Doughnut Economics

UPSC trap: Planetary Boundaries framework does NOT set legal limits — it is a scientific framework; it is NOT the same as the ecological footprint metric or carrying capacity regulations in Indian environmental law
